messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Graphic Designer
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Intrusive Thoughts: Unwanted thoughts, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Authority Presence: Police
  Maladaptive Strategies: Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking, Avoid People: avoid other people, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

The morning of the incident, Marcus had been finishing a late shift at the design studio, the only one left on the fourth floor of the converted warehouse downtown. He was packing his tablet when he heard the commotion from the street—shouting, then the screech of tires. He looked out the window and saw a patrol car angled across the intersection, doors open. Two officers were struggling with a man on the ground near a bodega. Marcus watched, frozen, as one officer’s knee pressed into the man’s back while the other swung a baton. He saw the man’s face go slack, then a bloom of red on the pavement beneath his head. Marcus didn’t look away. He couldn’t. He stood at that window for what felt like an hour, his coffee going cold in his hand, until another officer noticed him and shouted for him to step back. He stumbled to his desk and sat in the dark until the police tape came down.

That was eighteen months ago. Now, Marcus cannot see a police cruiser without his chest tightening. He takes three different routes to work to avoid the station two blocks from his office, and if he catches sight of a uniform in a coffee shop or on the sidewalk, he will turn around and walk the other way, even if it makes him late. He has stopped going to the grocery store near his apartment because a man with a scarred cheek works the register, and the sight of any visible injury—a bandage, a bruise, a healing cut—drops him straight back to that night. He will be standing in the cereal aisle, and suddenly he is at the window again, watching the blood spread, and his hands start to shake and his vision goes narrow. He has learned to keep his eyes on the floor in public, to scan only the lower halves of people’s bodies so he won’t catch a glimpse of a wound or a uniform.

At home, Marcus spends hours on his phone, scrolling through design feeds or playing matching games, because the moment he puts it down the thoughts come. He has become an expert at keeping his mind occupied. He listens to podcasts while he showers, has the television on while he eats dinner, and falls asleep with earbuds in. His wife, Lisa, has stopped trying to talk to him after nine o’clock because he cannot hold a conversation—he is too busy running a mental treadmill to keep the memory at bay. When she asked him last week what he was thinking about, he said nothing, which was true in the sense that he was working very hard to think of nothing at all.

But the memory does not wait for permission. It arrives without warning, triggered by something as small as the sound of a car door slamming or the particular quality of evening light through venetian blinds. When it comes, it is not a recollection—it is a full-body event. His heart hammers, his palms sweat, and he feels the same helpless horror he felt standing at that window. If he is in the middle of a sentence, he stops. He cannot finish. He has tried to tell Lisa what happened, twice, and both times he lost the thread halfway through, the words dissolving into a kind of static, and he ended up just shaking his head and walking away.

Marcus has come to believe that something essential in him was broken that night. He no longer finds pleasure in the work he used to love—the layouts feel hollow, the colors meaningless. He goes through the motions at his desk, meeting deadlines, but he cannot remember the last time he felt proud of a project. He is certain that his life has been fundamentally destroyed, that there is no version of himself that exists before the incident and no version that will exist after. What eats at him most is the injustice of it. He was just a bystander. He did nothing wrong. And yet he is the one who cannot sleep, who cannot sit in a restaurant without his eyes tracking the exits, who feels his body hum with tension from the moment he wakes up until the moment he finally, exhaustedly, passes out. No one has been held accountable for what he saw. Nothing has been done.

What finally brought Marcus to seek help was a moment two weeks ago, when his nine-year-old daughter asked him to play catch in the backyard and he said no because he could hear a siren three blocks away and knew he would not be able to concentrate on the ball. He watched her face fall, and he felt a kind of terror that was different from the usual fear—a colder, clearer dread. He is afraid that he is disappearing, that the man he used to be has already been replaced by this vigilant, hollow version of himself. He does not know if he can get the old Marcus back. But he knows he cannot keep watching his daughter’s face fall.
